lessons.title: Overview of Sheet Metal Industry and Careers
lessons.body: Sheet metal work is the craft of cutting, bending, and assembling thin metal sheets into useful products. In Africa, this trade is everywhere: from the rooflines of Nairobi to the car bodies in Lagos, from cooking pots in Accra to ventilation ducts in Johannesburg. The industry serves construction, automotive, appliance manufacturing, and agriculture. A skilled sheet metal worker can find work in fabrication shops, on building sites, or as an independent artisan. Many start by repairing roofs, gutters, and water tanks. Others move into making custom furniture, signage, or even art. The demand is steady because metal is durable and recyclable. With basic tools and a small workspace, you can start your own business. For example, a simple metal box for a solar panel can sell for 5,000 to 15,000 shillings in East Africa. The key is to learn the fundamentals: measuring, cutting, bending, and joining. This module gives you that foundation. You will learn safety, tools, materials, and basic techniques. No prior experience is needed. All you need is patience and a willingness to practice. By the end, you will be able to make simple items like a dustpan, a funnel, or a small toolbox. These skills can lead to apprenticeships or self-employment. The sheet metal industry is growing as African cities expand and need roofing, ventilation, and transport. So, whether you want a job or to start a workshop, this trade offers real opportunities.

lessons.title: Safety Practices and Personal Protective Equipment
lessons.body: Sheet metal work involves sharp edges, heavy tools, and flying particles. Safety is not optional. Always wear personal protective equipment (PPE). For eyes, use safety glasses or goggles. Metal shards can blind you. For hands, wear leather gloves when handling sheet metal. Cotton gloves do not protect against cuts. For ears, use earplugs when hammering or using power tools. For feet, wear closed-toe leather boots. Never wear sandals. For body, wear a tight-fitting apron or overalls. Loose clothing can get caught in tools. Also, tie back long hair. Before starting, check your tools. A loose hammer head can fly off. A dull chisel can slip. Keep your work area clean. Metal scraps on the floor cause falls. Use a brush, not your hands, to clear shavings. When cutting, always cut away from your body. When bending, keep fingers clear of the brake. When soldering or welding, use a face shield and fire-resistant gloves. Have a fire extinguisher nearby. In many African workshops, ventilation is poor. If you are soldering, open windows or work outside. Fumes from galvanized metal are toxic. Never heat galvanized steel without a respirator. Also, be careful with electricity. Use grounded tools and avoid water. If you get a cut, clean it with soap and water, apply pressure, and cover it. Seek medical help if deep. Report all injuries. A safe worker is a productive worker. Make safety a habit from day one.

lessons.title: Basic Hand Tools and Their Uses
lessons.body: You do not need expensive machines to start sheet metal work. A few hand tools will get you far. First, a ball-peen hammer. The round end shapes metal, the flat end strikes. Use it to flatten, stretch, or rivet. Second, a mallet. A rubber or wooden mallet shapes metal without stretching it. Use it for bending soft metals like aluminum. Third, tin snips. These are scissors for metal. Get a straight-cut and a curved-cut pair. Straight snips cut straight lines; curved snips cut circles. Never cut thick steel with snips; use a hacksaw. Fourth, a hacksaw with 18 or 24 teeth per inch. Use it for cutting pipes, bolts, and thick sheet. Fifth, a file. A flat file smooths edges. A round file enlarges holes. Sixth, a center punch. This makes a dent so a drill bit does not wander. Seventh, a drill. A hand drill or electric drill with bits for metal. Use cutting oil. Eighth, a rivet gun. It joins metal with rivets. Ninth, a soldering iron. For thin metal, soldering joins seams. Tenth, a bench vise. It holds metal while you work. Also, a straightedge, a scriber, and a measuring tape. In Africa, you can buy these tools at markets or hardware stores. A basic set costs 50,000 to 100,000 shillings. Keep them clean and oiled. Store them in a toolbox. Learn to sharpen snips and drill bits. With these tools, you can make gutters, boxes, funnels, and more.

lessons.title: Introduction to Measuring and Layout Tools
lessons.body: Accurate measuring and layout are the difference between a product that works and scrap metal. You need three basic tools: a tape measure, a steel rule, and a scriber. A tape measure is flexible and retractable. Get one that is at least 5 meters long. It measures curves and long lengths. A steel rule is rigid. Use it for short, straight measurements. A scriber is a sharp-pointed tool that scratches metal. It marks where you will cut or bend. Never use a pencil; it rubs off. For layout, you also need a combination square, a protractor, and a divider. A combination square checks 90-degree angles and 45-degree angles. A protractor measures other angles. A divider transfers measurements and draws circles. To lay out a simple box, first measure and mark the length and width. Use a scriber and a steel rule. Then use a square to draw perpendicular lines. For a 90-degree bend, mark a line, then use a bending brake. For a circle, set the divider to the radius, place the point at the center, and scratch the circle. Always double-check your measurements. A 1 mm error can ruin a whole sheet. In Africa, many workshops use metric. So learn millimeters and centimeters. Practice on scrap metal. Draw a square, a rectangle, and a circle. Then cut them out. The more you practice, the better your eye. Remember: measure twice, cut once. That old saying saves money and metal.

lessons.title: Understanding Metal Types and Gauges
lessons.body: Sheet metal comes in different types and thicknesses. The most common in Africa are galvanized steel, mild steel, aluminum, copper, and stainless steel. Galvanized steel is coated with zinc to prevent rust. It is used for roofing, gutters, and ventilation. It is cheap and easy to work. Mild steel is strong and weldable. It rusts if not painted. Use it for structural parts. Aluminum is light and rust-resistant. It is softer and easier to bend. Use it for cooking pots, signage, and aircraft parts. Copper is expensive but conducts heat and electricity. Use it for roofing, gutters, and art. Stainless steel resists rust and heat. It is hard to cut and bend. Use it for kitchen equipment and medical tools. Thickness is measured by gauge. The higher the gauge number, the thinner the metal. For example, 16 gauge is about 1.5 mm thick. 24 gauge is about 0.6 mm. 30 gauge is about 0.3 mm. In Africa, common gauges are 24, 26, and 28 for roofing. 16 to 20 gauge for boxes and ducts. 10 to 14 gauge for heavy-duty work. To choose a gauge, think about strength and weight. Thicker metal is stronger but heavier and harder to bend. Thinner metal is lighter but dents easily. Always check the gauge before buying. Use a gauge wheel or a micrometer. Practice bending different gauges to feel the difference. Start with 24 gauge galvanized steel. It is affordable and forgiving.

lessons.title: Shop Safety and Hazard Identification
lessons.body: A safe shop is a productive shop. Before you start work, walk around and spot hazards. Look for sharp edges on metal sheets. They can cut you even if you just brush against them. Always deburr edges with a file. Look for trip hazards like cables, scraps, and tools on the floor. Keep floors clean and dry. Look for fire hazards. Oily rags can self-ignite. Store them in a metal bin with a lid. Flammable liquids like paint thinner must be in sealed containers away from heat. Look for electrical hazards. Frayed cords, overloaded sockets, and water near electricity. Use circuit breakers. Look for poor ventilation. Soldering and welding produce toxic fumes. Work near an open window or use a fan. Look for improper tool use. A wrench used as a hammer can slip and injure. Use the right tool for the job. Also, identify emergency exits and first aid kits. Know where the fire extinguisher is and how to use it. In many African workshops, space is tight. So organize your work area. Keep a clear path. Store metal vertically or on racks. Never stack heavy sheets on the floor where someone can trip. Train everyone in basic first aid. For cuts, apply pressure and clean. For burns, cool with water. For eye injuries, flush with water and seek help. Hold a short safety meeting every week. Discuss near-misses. Learn from them. Safety is a habit, not a one-time event.

quiz.q: What is sheet metal work?
options: A) Working with thick metal bars
B) Cutting, bending, and assembling thin metal sheets
quiz.explanation: Sheet metal work involves thin sheets, not thick bars or only welding.

quiz.q: Which industry in Africa commonly uses sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Roofing and construction are major users of sheet metal in Africa.

quiz.q: What can a beginner make after learning basic sheet metal skills?
quiz.explanation: A dustpan is a simple project for beginners.

quiz.q: Why is safety important in sheet metal work?
options: B) Because metal is sharp and tools are dangerous
quiz.explanation: Sharp edges and tools can cause serious injuries.

quiz.q: Which PPE protects your eyes?
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses protect eyes from flying particles.

quiz.q: What type of gloves should you wear when handling sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Leather gloves resist cuts better than cotton or latex.

quiz.q: What should you do before using a hammer?
options: A) Check if the head is loose
quiz.explanation: A loose hammer head can fly off and cause injury.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important when soldering galvanized metal?
quiz.explanation: Heating galvanized metal releases toxic zinc fumes.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to shape metal without stretching it?
quiz.explanation: A rubber or wooden mallet shapes without stretching.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a center punch?
options: B) To make a dent for drilling
quiz.explanation: A center punch creates a starting point for a drill bit.

quiz.q: Which snips are used for cutting circles?
quiz.explanation: Curved snips are designed for cutting curves.

quiz.q: What should you use to cut thick steel?
quiz.explanation: A hacksaw with proper teeth per inch cuts thick steel.

quiz.q: What is a scriber used for?
quiz.explanation: A scriber marks metal with a sharp point.

quiz.q: Why should you not use a pencil to mark metal?
quiz.explanation: Pencil marks rub off during handling.

quiz.q: What does a combination square check?
quiz.explanation: A combination square checks right angles and 45-degree angles.

quiz.q: What is the rule for measuring and cutting?
quiz.explanation: Measuring twice reduces errors and waste.

quiz.q: Which metal is coated with zinc to prevent rust?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized steel has a zinc coating for rust resistance.

quiz.q: Which metal is light and rust-resistant?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum is lightweight and naturally resists rust.

quiz.q: What does a higher gauge number mean?
quiz.explanation: Higher gauge numbers indicate thinner sheets.

quiz.q: Which gauge is commonly used for roofing in Africa?
quiz.explanation: 24 gauge is a common thickness for roofing sheets.

quiz.q: What is a hazard in the shop?
quiz.explanation: Sharp edges can cause cuts and are a hazard.

quiz.q: How should oily rags be stored?
options: A) In a pile on the floor
B) In a metal bin with a lid
quiz.explanation: Oily rags can self-ignite; a metal bin with lid is safe.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get a cut?
options: B) Clean it and apply pressure
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and pressure help stop bleeding and prevent infection.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep floors clean?
options: B) To prevent trips and falls
quiz.explanation: Scraps and tools on the floor cause falls.

quiz.q: What should you do before starting work?
quiz.explanation: A hazard check prevents accidents.

quiz.q: Which tool holds metal while you work?
quiz.explanation: A bench vise securely holds metal.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a divider?
options: B) To transfer measurements and draw circles
quiz.explanation: A divider transfers distances and draws arcs.

quiz.q: Which metal is best for cooking pots?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum conducts heat well and is lightweight.

quiz.q: What should you use to deburr sharp edges?
quiz.explanation: A file smooths sharp edges.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of fires in workshops?
quiz.explanation: Oily rags can spontaneously combust.
